The Education

Why Dermatology Billing Requires Three Simultaneous Competencies

Medical billing, surgical coding, and cosmetic-to-medical routing each require distinct expertise. Dermatology practices with mixed service lines need all three simultaneously, without error.

Dermatology billing is the process of coding and submitting insurance claims for medical dermatology services, surgical skin procedures, and in practices with cosmetic services correctly separating what is medically billable from what is self-pay only. The complexity is threefold: the surgical coding, the medical-cosmetic boundary, and the biologic management billing program.

Mohs surgery is the highest-value and most commonly miscoded surgical procedure in dermatology. Mohs (CPT 17311-17315) is billed by the stage each stage requires the surgeon to personally perform the tissue excision, histologic processing, and microscopic examination. Stage 1 (17311 for head/neck/hands/feet/genitalia, 17313 for trunk/extremities) is followed by add-on codes (17312 or 17314) for each additional stage. The repair component intermediate or complex wound closure is billed separately. Missing any add-on stage code, billing the wrong anatomic code for the site, or failing to separately code the repair on complex closures leaves $400 to $1,200 per Mohs case uncaptured.

The medical vs. cosmetic billing distinction is the compliance centerpiece of dermatology billing. A sebaceous cyst removal driven by infection or pain is a medical procedure billed to insurance. The same sebaceous cyst removed for cosmetic reasons is self-pay. BOTOX for blepharospasm is a medical procedure billed with J0585 and supporting diagnosis codes. BOTOX for facial wrinkles is cosmetic self-pay. Incorrectly billing a cosmetic procedure to insurance creates false claims act exposure. Incorrectly routing a medical procedure to self-pay means the patient pays out of pocket for covered care. PMEx maintains procedure-by-procedure classification rules updated per payer and per procedure type.

Biologic prior authorization for psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, and hidradenitis suppurativa requires clinical documentation of disease severity, prior conventional therapy failure, and body surface area or validated severity scores. PMEx manages all biologic auth workflows for dermatology secukinumab, ixekizumab, guselkumab, risankizumab, dupilumab, and adalimumab with step therapy documentation built for each payer's specific requirements.

The Single Most Dangerous Distinction in Dermatology Billing

The Medical vs. Cosmetic Billing Line

Every dermatology practice with mixed medical and cosmetic services faces the same compliance centerpiece: correctly determining which procedures are medically billable and which are self-pay only. The distinction is determined by medical necessity documentation, diagnosis codes, and payer-specific coverage policies not by the procedure itself. The same procedure can be medical or cosmetic depending entirely on why it is being performed.

Crossing the line in the wrong direction creates two different problems. Billing a cosmetic procedure to insurance a wrinkle injection coded as a medical service, a cosmetic skin lesion removal submitted with a medical diagnosis is insurance fraud, regardless of intent. Audit, recoupment, and in severe cases qui tam exposure follow systematic cosmetic-to-insurance billing. The other direction creates a different problem: routing a medically necessary procedure to self-pay charges the patient for covered care. Both are wrong. Both are common in dermatology practices without dedicated billing oversight.

PMEx maintains a procedure-by-procedure medical-cosmetic classification matrix updated for every major payer's coverage policies. Every dermatology charge is classified before routing medical procedures to insurance with correct diagnosis support, cosmetic procedures to self-pay invoicing. Zero medical-cosmetic routing errors on any PMEx-managed dermatology practice.

Mohs Stage Error

Mohs Add-On Stage Codes Not Applied

Three-stage Mohs surgery on the nose. 17311 applied for Stage 1. 17312 add-on for Stages 2 and 3 never submitted. $1,080 in add-on stage revenue lost. Repair billed as simple rather than complex closure additional $380 per case.

PMEx reviews every Mohs operative report for stage count and repair complexity. 17312 or 17314 applied for each additional stage. Repair coded at the correct complexity level from the closure documentation.

Excision Margin Error

Wrong Excision Code for Lesion Size/Margin

Melanoma in situ excised with 1.0 cm margin on the forearm. Correct code: 11604 (excision, trunk/extremities, 2.1-3.0 cm). Coded as 11602 (1.1-2.0 cm). $185 per case reimbursement differential missed because the margin calculation was not added to the lesion diameter before code selection.

PMEx calculates excision code based on the lesion diameter PLUS margin on each side per CMS definition. The correct excision code is selected from the operative report capturing the actual tissue removed, not just the lesion size.

Biologic Auth Lapse

Psoriasis Biologic Administered Without Active Auth

Patient on secukinumab for plaque psoriasis. Prior authorization expired. Drug administered. Payer denies the drug billing retroactively. $8,000 to $12,000 biologic claim lost. Drug already administered, patient outcome already delivered, revenue permanently gone.

PMEx tracks biologic authorization renewal cycles for every patient submitting renewals 30 days before expiration. Every drug administration has active confirmed authorization. Zero biologic administration proceeds without active coverage confirmed in advance.

Phototherapy Code Error

Phototherapy Sessions Under-Coded

Narrowband UVB phototherapy sessions billed as office visits rather than the correct procedure code (96900 for actinotherapy/phototherapy). Reimbursement difference: $45 to $85 per session. Three sessions per week, 52 weeks, multiple patients systematic underbilling accumulates to $20K to $40K annually.

PMEx codes phototherapy sessions with the correct procedure code for each therapy type narrowband UVB (96900), PUVA (96912), and excimer laser (96920-96922) billed with the correct intensity documentation and diagnosis codes.

Cosmetic Coding Compliance

Cosmetic Procedures Billed to Insurance

Billing team applies medical diagnosis codes to cosmetic procedures to route them through insurance billing. Payer recoups on audit. Or: medical dermatology manager is unaware the billing team is submitting cosmetic charges to insurance. Systematic false claims act exposure created without clinical awareness.

PMEx applies the medical-cosmetic classification check before every charge. No insurance submission proceeds without confirmed medical necessity diagnosis documentation. Cosmetic procedures are automatically routed to patient self-pay invoicing.

Skin Biopsy Coding Error

Multiple Biopsy Sites Under-Reported

Four punch biopsies performed at the same visit from different sites. Billed as a single 11104 code. Three additional biopsies (11105 add-on, $65 each) never submitted. $195 per multi-biopsy visit lost. Happens consistently across dozens of visits per month in dermatology practices with high biopsy volumes.

PMEx identifies the biopsy count from the procedure note and applies 11104 for the first site plus 11105 add-on codes for each additional site. Every biopsy at every site is captured and billed on every multi-site visit.

PMEx calculates excision codes using the CMS definition: lesion diameter PLUS the narrowest margin on each side. If a lesion is 1.2 cm with 0.5 cm margins, the excised diameter is 1.2 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 2.2 cm placing it in the 2.1-3.0 cm code bracket rather than the 1.1-2.0 cm bracket. This margin-inclusive calculation is how CMS defines excision size, and most practices apply it incorrectly by using lesion size alone.

Yes. Phototherapy billing narrowband UVB (96900), PUVA (96912), excimer laser (96920-96922), and photodynamic therapy (96567/96573) requires correct procedure code selection based on the therapy type and treatment area, prior authorization from commercial payers for high-dose or extended treatment, and correct patient dose documentation. PMEx manages phototherapy billing as a complete recurring workflow for practices running phototherapy programs.
